Starfruit - 1 year, 23lbs, Kelpie/Aussie Mix, Spayed 

This dog is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Our Team Says: "Starfruit will do best in a home outside of the city. She's not cut out for this city thing. She's a wonderful dog - very sweet, fun and but her nervous system can't handle it here. If you live out of the city - this girl is a great fit for you. Starfuit daydreams about having a yard to call her own and a calm trail to walk." 

Thier Foster Parent Says: "Starfruit is a total love bug. She takes a minute to warm up to new people, but once she knows you, she'll be all over you!! Her favorite place is right next to me on the couch, and she'll roll over for belly rubs any chance she gets. Her favorite hobby is destroying her Lambchop toy, so just keep an eye out to make sure she doesn't swallow any squeakers or plastic pieces. She gets the zoomies three or four times a day, and they will make you fall in love with her! Inside the home she's a dream: reliably potty trained, comfortable in her crate, fine being left alone, and she gets along well with other dogs. City noise and activity startle her, which makes her anxious, so she prefers to keep her outdoor time short. She does much better in open, grassy spaces away from the hustle and bustle, and I think she'd truly blossom in a quieter home where she can relax."

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – This dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.)

Energy Level:
MEDIUM – Needs a daily 60-90 minute walk or window of quick paced exercise (minimum) in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). Also needs significant socializing opportunities outside the home and mental stimulation at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

POTTY TRAINING:
Yes, few or no accidents

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS:
Wallflower - shy with strangers, takes a second to warm up to new people. 

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN:
Okay for a home with kids aged 12 and up 

SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS:
Mostly. She tends to be neutral toward or ignore most dogs on the street, but gets curious She's still a little territorial. It's mostly around toys, and she can be a bit protective of me when I'm on the couch. She does respond well to correction, though it's definitely not mastered yet. That said, she's come a long way living with Scout. She's learned to play much better and is way more confident approaching dogs on the street. I think she'd do well with another dog as long as her new family keeps an eye on toys and furniture at first and stays consistent with correction. Probably best as a SOLO dog household but having a sibling not out of the question.

BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS:
Not sure

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR:
Past this stage with furniture and belongings. She does destroy her toys thoroughly, so she needs supervision to keep her from eating plastic parts or squeakers.

SEPARATION ANXIETY:
Past this stage

LEASH MANNERS:
Getting the hang of it

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL:
High

JUMPING ON PEOPLE:
Listens to correction. She never jumps on strangers, but she does jump on the people she loves when she's excited, and she responds to "Gentle."

CRATE TRAINING:
Yep/mostly

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from Tennessee or Puerto Rico; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses.

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

LEARN MORE ABOUT US: socialteesnyc.org and Instagram @socialteesnyc

Becky - 2 years & 12lbs, Maltese/Terrier Mix, Spayed 

This dog is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Our Team Says: " Becky needs a home outside of the city, she's not meant for the city life. We really want her with another dog buddy that can help her show the ropes." 

Level of dog ownership experience required:
JUST A REALLY PATIENT SOUL – Becky is a special fluff. She's extremely shy and is learning how to be a dog. She needs a lot of time to get comfy and a lot of grace. She's very gentle. We know there's a very special lady inside of her you're just not going to see it for a while. If you're okay with that, then this girl is for you. If you want a golden retriever personality on day one - not the girl for you. 

Energy level:
Lower  – Needs a daily 30 minute walk or window of quick paced exercise (minimum) in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). Also needs significant socializing opportunities outside the home and mental stimulation at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

Energy Level- She is very chill but will come by for some affection.  Most of the time she is happy in her doggy bed.

Tolerance to City-  Nope. Needs a home in the burbs. 

Potty Training-  Slowly getting the hang of it. She's decompressing still. But we know she'll get there. She's starting to pee outside. She only goes twice a day so she's predictable and wants to be a good girl, just feeling a little upside down. 

Comfort Level w/ Strangers- While she's still scared and shy, she is not an aggressive dog.  Even in her panic mode, she didn't try to nip or bite at anytime or showed any aggressive behavior.  She is very sweet.

Separation Anxiety- Nope, no sep anxiety/ She will sometimes follow me into other rooms when I move, but also fine on her own.  She has been left alone without much hovering the first few days so she can decompress.  She has not barked yet!

Leash Manners- She just shuts down and sits and starts shaking or lies down.  Can not get her to walk on the leash yet.

Cuddle Bug Level- Medium- Loves snuggles and belly rubs.  Very Sweet.

Crate Training- Loved the Crate.  It gives her a sense of safety.  She also loves her doggy beds.  She sleeps well in a crate at night.  Also in the soft carrier in the car.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from Tennessee or Puerto Rico; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake

pets.name: Milo
pets.description: Milo - 2 years, 20lbs, Chiweenie, Neutered Our Team Says: "This pup was rescued from a hoarding situation in PR - involving about 40 dogs. Due to this these pups are on the shyer side and need patient people who will give them time to get used to normal life. They are very sweet dogs: just need more time and patience. Milo needs a home with a yard - he only likes to do his business off leash and where he feels safe. He's a great walker though and not really scacred of the city, which is really awesome. Their Foster Family Says: " Milo is gradually adjusting to the city and I think he'll continue blossoming into a sweet, active dog with the support of other loving humans and canine buddies. His two greatest loves: sniffing dog pee outdoors (like REALLY huffing it) and curling up into a cinnamon roll in a pile of blankets. At home, he is mellow and observant. He likes to be in the same room as his humans, but he isn't (yet?) a snuggler and prefers his personal space. He hasn't taken an interest in toys, preferring instead to get comfy on any soft surface and watch the action around him. Outdoors, he is still a Nervous Nelly, keeping his tail tucked and remaining on high alert. He does pretty well on the leash, but if he gets spooked (shadows, rats, etc.) he will try to dart. We've had trouble getting him comfortable enough outdoors to go to the bathroom outside consistently (even with roasted chicken as his high-value reward); he typically holds it while we're outdoors and then goes on our balcony once we're home. He'd love a private outdoor space and a patient human who can continue working on potty training with him. He sleeps in a crate through the night without a peep, and does well home alone. He's a sweet, gentle dog who just needs some more time to adjust." ENERGY LEVEL Medium – Needs a daily 60-90 minute morning walk or window of quick paced exercise in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). Otherwise pretty chill indoors. Also needs significant opportunities to socialize outside the home and mental stimulation at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) TOLERANCE TO CITY Adjusting to the cit y – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). Would prefer a home in a calmer part of the city or the suburbs. POTTY TRAINING Yes - just needs a yard :) COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS Wallflower – Very shy with new people and takes a while to warm up. Afraid when unfamiliar people try to say hi on the street, hides or shrinks back when new people visit the home. BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision) Maybe for age 12 and up – Is either big and energetic (okay with kids big enough not to get knocked down) or a little skittish (could be comfortable with older children that can be extra gentle) SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS Mostly – Generally good with other dogs but may be selective (scared of big dogs or plays too rough for small dogs, for example) — Hesitant around dogs on the street, typically retreats but occasionally shows curiosity RESPECTFUL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS (cats, small pets, etc.) Yes - okay for a home with cats, doesn't mind them MOUTHY BEHAVIOR Past this stage– Little to no interest in chewing on stuff or putting things in their mouth that aren’t food. Doesn’t try to chew on hands, feet, etc. during playtime SEPARATION ANXIETY (Please leave your foster dog home alone every day for at least 20 minutes.) Past this stage – Completely fine being left home alone. Doesn’t cry or exhibit destructive behavior when you leave the apartment or house. LEASH MANNERS Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. CUDDLE BUG LEVEL Lower – Independent, mostly keeps to themself (may be a new rescue or shy, this could change) JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on the floor. CRATE TRAINING Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night. Medical status: Healthy for their age as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from Tennessee or Puerto Rico; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. Adopters will need to be ready for senior care – at a minimum, that will be annual checkups including senior bloodwork and a dental post adoption (most senior rescues need one). How did this dog end up with Social Tees? Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. pets.descriptionHtml:
Milo - 2 years, 20lbs, Chiweenie, Neutered

Our Team Says: "This pup was rescued from a hoarding situation in PR - involving about 40 dogs. Due to this these pups are on the shyer side and need patient people who will give them time to get used to normal life. They are very sweet dogs: just need more time and patience. Milo needs a home with a yard - he only likes to do his business off leash and where he feels safe. He's a great walker though and not really scacred of the city, which is really awesome.

Their Foster Family Says: "Milo is gradually adjusting to the city and I think he'll continue blossoming into a sweet, active dog with the support of other loving humans and canine buddies. His two greatest loves: sniffing dog pee outdoors (like REALLY huffing it) and curling up into a cinnamon roll in a pile of blankets. At home, he is mellow and observant. He likes to be in the same room as his humans, but he isn't (yet?) a snuggler and prefers his personal space. He hasn't taken an interest in toys, preferring instead to get comfy on any soft surface and watch the action around him. Outdoors, he is still a Nervous Nelly, keeping his tail tucked and remaining on high alert. He does pretty well on the leash, but if he gets spooked (shadows, rats, etc.) he will try to dart. We've had trouble getting him comfortable enough outdoors to go to the bathroom outside consistently (even with roasted chicken as his high-value reward); he typically holds it while we're outdoors and then goes on our balcony once we're home. He'd love a private outdoor space and a patient human who can continue working on potty training with him. He sleeps in a crate through the night without a peep, and does well home alone. He's a sweet, gentle dog who just needs some more time to adjust."

ENERGY LEVEL
Medium – Needs a daily 60-90 minute morning walk or window of quick paced exercise in addition to potty break strolls (10-30 min each). Otherwise pretty chill indoors. Also needs significant opportunities to socialize outside the home and mental stimulation at home like tricks training practice, chew items, and puzzle toys. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.)

TOLERANCE TO CITY
Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). Would prefer a home in a calmer part of the city or the suburbs.

POTTY TRAINING
Yes - just needs a yard :) 

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
Wallflower – Very shy with new people and takes a while to warm up. Afraid when unfamiliar people try to say hi on the street, hides or shrinks back when new people visit the home.

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)
Maybe for age 12 and up – Is either big and energetic (okay with kids big enough not to get knocked down) or a little skittish (could be comfortable with older children that can be extra gentle)

SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS
Mostly – Generally good with other dogs but may be selective (scared of big dogs or plays too rough for small dogs, for example) — Hesitant around dogs on the street, typically retreats but occasionally shows curiosity

RESPECTFUL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS (cats, small pets, etc.)
Yes - okay for a home with cats, doesn't mind them 

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Past this stage– Little to no interest in chewing on stuff or putting things in their mouth that aren’t food. Doesn’t try to chew on hands, feet, etc. during playtime

SEPARATION ANXIETY (Please leave your foster dog home alone every day for at least 20 minutes.)
Past this stage – Completely fine being left home alone. Doesn’t cry or exhibit destructive behavior when you leave the apartment or house.

LEASH MANNERS
Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction.

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Lower – Independent, mostly keeps to themself (may be a new rescue or shy, this could change)

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Calm Greetings – Doesn’t jump up on people or dogs. Always all four on the floor.

CRATE TRAINING
Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night.

Medical status:
Healthy for their age as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from Tennessee or Puerto Rico; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. Adopters will need to be ready for senior care – at a minimum, that will be annual checkups including senior bloodwork and a dental post adoption (most senior rescues need one).

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses.

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

LEARN MORE ABOUT US: socialteesnyc.org and Instagram @socialteesnyc

Thier Foster Parent Says: "This sweet girl is playful, curious, and goofy, but once she settles down, she’s a total cuddle bug. She loves playing tug, chewing her favorite bones, and watching birds on walks. Ruby is great in her crate, wonderful with new people, playful with other dogs, and doesn’t bark much at all. She can be a little shy when she first meets someone, but her friendly, curious personality quickly shines through once she feels comfortable. She’s still just a baby and is growing into her personality every day! Ruby is a spunky little puppy. She is equally calm as she is curious. Ruby would do well in an environment with another pup to show her the ropes and somewhere with some space to run! She’s a very curious pup and loves to people watch. I think Ruby would make the perfect companion!!”"

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Sort of -- On the way and learning! May be using wee pads (is a puppy or a brand new rescue)

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
In between bean – Fine with meeting new people but not particularly interested, kind of shy in busy social situations like a gathering or a packed day in the park.

Social with dogs?
Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)
Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc.

Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction.

Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Needs training – Very excited to greet everyone and has no idea how to do so politely. Jumps up on most strangers or other dogs that go by. In puppy phase or wasn’t trained as a young adult.

CRATE TRAINING
Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives.

She would be happiest in a home that has a yard. Her current foster parent has a yard and has no problems with her regarding to potty stuff."

Thier Foster Parent Says: "Butternut is an athletic sweetheart. She loves to jump, play tug-o-war, and play catch. She is warming to the city, the sounds bother her less, she’s intrigued by the sights and wants to explore however, still only does her business in the privacy of her own backyard-she’s a lady. We’ve ditched the bowl and use a puzzle ball for breakfast and dinner. It’s especially good first thing in the morning after her morning potty. She's still learning how to be fully comfortable home alone."

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

TOLERANCE TO CITY
Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). Would prefer a home in a calmer part of the city or the suburbs.

POTTY TRAINING
Yes - few or no accidents. - Only uses backyard.

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
In between bean – Fine with meeting new people but not particularly interested, kind of shy in busy social situations like a gathering or a packed day in the park. And wants to be friends with everyone who walks by.

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)
Maybe for age 12 and up – Is either big and energetic (okay with kids big enough not to get knocked down) or a little skittish (could be comfortable with older children that can be extra gentle)

SOCIAL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER DOGS
Mostly – Generally good with other dogs but may be selective (scared of big dogs or plays too rough for small dogs, for example)

RESPECTFUL BEHAVIOR WITH OTHER ANIMALS (cats, small pets, etc.)
Not sure – Wants to chase squirrels and birds so may not be a good match for a home with cats, rabbits, etc.

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc.

SEPARATION ANXIETY (Please leave your foster dog home alone every day for at least 20 minutes.)
Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise.

LEASH MANNERS
Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction.

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Listens to correction – Only jumps on people they know when really excited, stops with correction.

CRATE TRAINING
Working on it - We set one up and leave the door open but rarely close it because the dog freaks out

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives.

Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up.

Social with dogs?  

Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)  

Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. 

Social with cats?  

Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

Mouthy play:   

High! All puppies go through phases where they chew your stuff and grab your hands, arms, feet… puppies naturally explore the world, play, and test boundaries with their mouths. (It also happens when they’re teething.) Their teeth are super sharp, so it can be a very painful phase for humans and other animals in the home. Proper training, outlets, and socialization are key.

Separation anxiety:  

Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

Leash manners:  

None or learning, depending on the puppy’s age. Will need to work on this skill. 

Crate trained?  

Probably not. None of our new puppies have been formally trained, but many of our foster parents/adopters choose to crate train so some of the puppies that have been with us for a little while are learning this skill. It can be a great way to keep puppies safe and teach them independence.

Medical status:  

Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?  

Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

pets.name: Benjamin
pets.description: Benjamin - 4 months & 20lbs, Chi/Terrier Mix, Neutered Estimated full grown size around 30lbs This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Level of dog ownership experience required: INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult. Energy level: MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) Potty trained? Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up. Social with dogs? Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. Social with children? (ALWAYS requires adult supervision) Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. Social with cats? Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. Mouthy play: High! All puppies go through phases where they chew your stuff and grab your hands, arms, feet… puppies naturally explore the world, play, and test boundaries with their mouths. (It also happens when they’re teething.) Their teeth are super sharp, so it can be a very painful phase for humans and other animals in the home. Proper training, outlets, and socialization are key. Separation anxiety: Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial. Leash manners: None or learning, depending on the puppy’s age. Will need to work on this skill. Crate trained? Probably not. None of our new puppies have been formally trained, but many of our foster parents/adopters choose to crate train so some of the puppies that have been with us for a little while are learning this skill. It can be a great way to keep puppies safe and teach them independence. Medical status: Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.) How did this dog end up with Social Tees? Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Estimated full grown size around 30lbs 

This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

Potty trained?
Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up.

Social with dogs?
Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)
Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. 

Social with cats?
Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

Mouthy play: 
High! All puppies go through phases where they chew your stuff and grab your hands, arms, feet… puppies naturally explore the world, play, and test boundaries with their mouths. (It also happens when they’re teething.) Their teeth are super sharp, so it can be a very painful phase for humans and other animals in the home. Proper training, outlets, and socialization are key.

Separation anxiety:
Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

Leash manners:
None or learning, depending on the puppy’s age. Will need to work on this skill. 

Crate trained?
Probably not. None of our new puppies have been formally trained, but many of our foster parents/adopters choose to crate train so some of the puppies that have been with us for a little while are learning this skill. It can be a great way to keep puppies safe and teach them independence.

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

He also loves his person a lot and is still learning that being by himself is okay, he’s definitely the kind of puppy who wants to be wherever you are! Everything is still new and exciting to Jangle, and he’s just beginning to figure out the world around him. For someone who has the patience and time to dedicate to puppy training, Jangle will reward you with an incredibly happy, curious, affectionate little companion who is a giant love bug."

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

TOLERANCE TO CITY
City pup – Seems unfazed by the sights and sounds, may as well have been born here.

Potty trained?
Working on this skill. Puppies under 12 weeks old are often on track with their wee pad skills, but they’re too young to walk outside in public NYC areas yet because they haven’t finished their puppy vaccine series. Puppies older than 12 weeks are usually learning to do their business outside. Potty training takes a lot of patience, consistency, and clean up.

Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to.

Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. 

Social with cats?
Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
In between bean  – Fine with meeting new people but not particularly interested, kind of shy in busy social situations like a gathering or a packed day in the park. 

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc. 

Separation anxiety:
Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes at night or when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

LEASH MANNERS
Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. 

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
High – Wants to be in your lap pretty much all the time

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Needs training – Very excited to greet everyone and has no idea how to do so politely. Jumps up on most strangers or other dogs that go by. In puppy phase or wasn’t trained as a young adult.

CRATE TRAINING
Working on it – We set one up and leave the door open but rarely close it because the dog freaks out

Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives.

High – Wants to be in your lap pretty much all the time

Listens to correction – Only jumps on people they know when really excited, stops with correction.

CRATE TRAINING
Working on it – We set one up and leave the door open but rarely close it because the dog freaks out

Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

Expected to be about 45lbs full grown

Thier Foster Parent Says: "Charlie is a super sweet puppy!  He gets along so well with my 75 lb boxer and they play periodically throughout the day.  He his easily correctible if my dog is done playing, Charlie bows down and stops. He has a medium level of energy, is fully ready to play everytime we go outside into the yard, and is equally ready to chill and sleep. He is just learning to play with toys and people, but loves to play and wrestle with other dogs. We live upstate Ny so how he is in the city I would not know. But he loves running and rolling in the grass, loves to dig in the dirt a little, and loves to grab a slipper here and there. He is very good about relieving himself outside every time I put him out to play and he has only had two pee accidents because I was not seeing his pee signs before hand. He also knows the word ‘no’ and sit and does both very well. He loves treats and takes them very gently. He is super sweet with new people and will run up to them right away, but a little timid to let you fully touch him as it seems he doen’t immediately like to be picked up. I have not walked him on a leash yet but will do in the next day or two to see how he does -it is all new to him so inside the house, he pulls a little when you try to guide him with the leash – he is not used to this at all yet. I have not seen him with children yet but I feel he will be gentle and like them as he does adults so far – he is not jumpy and nippy at all. He has slept through the night every night since I have had him, without crying or needing to pee. He sleeps in his bed on the floor next to mine and is not needy at all.
 He loves his crate and has not problem going In for a nap, snack or when I have to leave the house. He did not cry at all when I left.
 If I have to leave the house more than 4 hours (which has been one time) he is perfectly content in his crate wth a kong of peanut butter and greeting our dog ‘walker’ eagerly when she came in at the midway mark. He was super friendly and they went out intot he fenced yard for. A half and hour to play. She had no issue getting him back in the crate inticed with a pig ear. He jumps a little bit when excited, but he stops the minute you tell him to. He does not need a ton of cuddles and will not get on the couch or bed unless you bring him up, but he will cuddle if you cuddle him – he is not needy so far."

(This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

Potty trained?
Yes - Charlie is crushing this! 

Social with dogs?
Yes. Some puppies are shy, others are bold, but all have the potential to be taught healthy socializing skills. It’s a huge part of raising a puppy and must be done carefully. How they interact with other dogs depends largely on how their humans help them learn to. 

Social with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision)
Sort of – some puppies enjoy interacting with children, others get easily overwhelmed by their energy and attention. Regardless, most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. Charlie seems like a good fit for a home with kids. 

Social with cats?
Yes. Most puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

Mouthy play: 
Charlie is doing really well with this. He is not super mouthy at all. 

Separation anxiety:
Nope - Charlie is fine left home alone. Good at self soothing. 

Leash manners:
Learning how to walk on a leash. He was rescued for the USVI and was an off-leash dog. 

Crate trained?
Yes - doing great in a crate. 

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives.

Their foster says: "If Joey could have it his way, he'd spend most of the day nuzzled under your chin, curled in your lap, or stretched out in the crook of your arm, with the rest of the time for big walks and saying hi to dogs. He can't always have it his way, so he's happy to wait patiently for you to come do one of those things. Joey is a total cuddlebug sweetheart who loves his person and wants to be close. He loves saying hi to other dogs and is polite, if a little awkward, and I think will be eager to play with the right dog friend. Don't be fooled by his age! He has wonderful puppy-like energy and has not yet met a hike that has bested him, and loves to get his zoomies out playing with his people. He is readily gaining confidence in the city but is still pretty spooked by cars, so would really shine in a more suburban area. He can be slow to warm up to some men. Joey really is a spunky little lovebug."

Level of dog ownership experience needed:  

FLEXIBLE – We predict this dog will be low on the challenge scale with regard to exercise and mental stimulation requirements, but seniors tend to need a lot of help and understanding when it comes to lifestyle and veterinary issues. Seniors usually need quiet, calm environments and routines and do not do well with a lot of bustle, change, and rambunctious movement (kids and young playful dogs, for instance). This dog’s adopter will need to be prepared for senior health challenges, which means frequent vet visits and very expensive veterinary bills. (An annual senior blood panel alone costs around $500 in NYC.) Senior care can also take an emotional toll on their humans. Adopting a mature pup is a wonderful thing to do, but it can also be difficult.

Energy level:  

LOWER – Pretty chill indoors and won’t demand endless amounts of stimulation and exercise but still needs a few short walks a day (10-30 min each) for potty breaks and to stretch their legs. His foster said, "He is totally up for higher-intensity adventures but doesn't need it. We went for a long steep hike and he loved it."

Okay in the city?  

Adjusting – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). Would prefer a home in a calmer part of the city or the suburbs.

Potty trained? Yes – Few or no accidents - he can hold it while home alone but doesn't cue to go out when you're home and can have accidents.

Social with other dogs? Yes – Good with most other dogs (sizes, breeds, etc.) as far as we know and enjoys socializing with other canines - wants to say hi to every dog but is pretty awkward/shy when he does

Comfort level with strangers: Social butterfly! Wants to be friends with everyone who walks by, loves anyone who will stop to say hello. Doesn't like some men, barks and growls, but gets used to them eventually

Social with cats? Yes – Seems to get along with cats etc., either tries to play with them or is mostly uninterested - more scared than anything, in a respectful and curious way.

Comfortable with children?  (ALWAYS requires adult supervision): Yes for most ages – very confident, gentle, low energy, tolerant, not mouthy. HIs foster reports, "I have not spent a lot of time with a kid but he has met toddlers in the park and been very gentle."

Mouthy behavior? Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc. - will eat underwear and grab chicken bones off the street. can be very gently mouthy while playing.

Leash manners:   

Old Pro – Doesn’t pull hard or need much direction.

Separation anxiety? Adjusting – Might cry for a few minutes when you first leave the house but settles pretty quickly and has no problem being left alone otherwise.

Cuddle bug level:   

High – Wants to be in your lap pretty much all the time

Jumping on people to say hello?   

Listens to correction – Only jumps on people they know when really excited, stops with correction.

Past this stage – Completely fine being left home alone.

Between medium and high. He loves to cuddle but will also have some alone time snoozing in the other room.

pets.description: Chance - 3 months & 21lbs (as of 10/1), Pointer Mix, Neutered This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Our Team Says: "Chance has so much love to give that his heart can't contain it all. Chance had an Echo in October to make sure his heart was okay as it sounded a little abnormal during his exam. Good news - he has PFO - it's where the flap between his chambers hasn't fully closed properly yet. Usually it closes after birth but he's extra special and his didn't fully close fully. The cardiologist wasn't worried at all though and was pretty certain that it will close. He suggested doing an echo in 6 months from now to just to triple check." Thier Foster Parent Says: "Chance is the loveliest pup ever! He’s smart, clean, observant, playful, and absolutely loves people. He enjoys adventure walks and gets so excited when he meets other dogs and humans. In a new neighborhood, Chance can get a little overwhelmed by noise and all the movement from cars and people. Once he gets the hang of the neighborhood hustle and bustle, he loves to explore. At home, he loves a good daytime nap! His forever home would ideally have an outdoor garden where he can go potty in a quiet, familiar space. He seems to prefer having a little area to himself, with fewer distractions and no leash. On walks, he can get distracted by everything around him, so he needs a little extra time and encouragement to focus on going potty. He’s getting the hang of it, though! Chance is such a sweet, curious boy, and with a little patience, consistency, and lots of love, he’ll continue to thrive." Level of dog ownership experience required: INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Chance - 3 months & 21lbs (as of 10/1), Pointer Mix, Neutered 

This puppy is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application at socialteesnyc.org

Our Team Says: "Chance has so much love to give that his heart can't contain it all. Chance had an Echo in October to make sure his heart was okay as it sounded a little abnormal during his exam. Good news - he has PFO - it's where the flap between his chambers hasn't fully closed properly yet. Usually it closes after birth but he's extra special and his didn't fully close fully. The cardiologist wasn't worried at all though and was pretty certain that it will close. He suggested doing an echo in 6 months from now to just to triple check." 

Thier Foster Parent Says: "Chance is the loveliest pup ever! He’s smart, clean, observant, playful, and absolutely loves people. He enjoys adventure walks and gets so excited when he meets other dogs and humans. In a new neighborhood, Chance can get a little overwhelmed by noise and all the movement from cars and people. Once he gets the hang of the neighborhood hustle and bustle, he loves to explore. At home, he loves a good daytime nap! His forever home would ideally have an outdoor garden where he can go potty in a quiet, familiar space. He seems to prefer having a little area to himself, with fewer distractions and no leash. On walks, he can get distracted by everything around him, so he needs a little extra time and encouragement to focus on going potty. He’s getting the hang of it, though! Chance is such a sweet, curious boy, and with a little patience, consistency, and lots of love, he’ll continue to thrive."

Level of dog ownership experience required:
INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. The adopter must have relevant primary care experience with a similar breed, temperament, and/or energy level. (Primary care experience includes ownership, fostering, or dog sitting as an adult, not a dog you grew up with.) Relevant puppy care experience is a huge plus, but bare minimum the adopter must have TONS of time and patience. Raising a puppy can be a lot of fun, but it’s also  tremendous work. Puppies’ personalities and exercise/stimulation requirements change dramatically between now and when they’re a year old as their bodies and brains develop, so an active lifestyle and the ability to adapt to a pup’s evolving needs are a must. We strongly urge professional dog training with a rewards based trainer from the get go. Adults only or kids ages 8 and up – all puppies go through a mouthy, rambunctious phase and often accidentally hurt children when playing. PLEASE DO YOUR OWN BREED RESEARCH to make sure you have a better understanding of the kind of temperament and exercise requirements this dog may have as an adult.

Energy level:
MEDIUM – Very young puppies sleep and nap a lot, but their energy level skyrockets when they become teens (4 months to around a year). As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day at a minimum. (This is regardless of dog size – many small breeds were designed for lots of activity and will exhibit unwanted behavior when they’re understimulated.) 

TOLERANCE TO CITY
Adjusting to the city – Spooked easily by loud noises and bustling areas but walks pretty well in quiet areas and probably just needs more time to adjust (may be a puppy or a brand new rescue). 

POTTY TRAINING:
Yes – Few or no accidents

COMFORT LEVEL WITH STRANGERS
Social butterfly – Wants to be friends with everyone who walks by, loves anyone who will stop to say hello. 

BEHAVIOR WITH CHILDREN (always requires adult supervision)
Yes… but most puppies are not a great match for a home with kids under age 8 because they go through intense mouthy play and rambunctious phases and often accidentally hurt young kids while playing. Children must always be monitored and taught to interact with dogs of any age respectfully. 

Social with cats?
Yes. Almost all puppies have the potential to be friends with a cat. It’s on the adopter to know their cat’s temperament and preferences and to teach their puppy respectful manners. 

MOUTHY BEHAVIOR
Working on it – Is respectful of hands, feet, etc. but likes to chew on things they’re not supposed to like shoes, furniture, etc. 

SEPARATION ANXIETY
 Most puppies have some level of separation anxiety as they learn to self soothe. Often they cry the first 10+ minutes when they are left home alone or in a crate. Consistent training and alone time is crucial.

LEASH MANNERS
Getting the hang of it – Probably hasn’t been on a leash much in their life but figuring it out. Might be a mild puller but responds to correction. 

CUDDLE BUG LEVEL
Medium – Likes to snuggle when he's in the mood but often stays in his own bed

JUMPING ON PEOPLE TO SAY HELLO
Needs training – Very excited to greet everyone and has no idea how to do so politely. Jumps up on most strangers or other dogs that go by. In puppy phase or wasn’t trained as a young adult. 

CRATE TRAINING
Yep/mostly – Seems comfortable in the crate, may whine a little at first but settles pretty quickly. We use the crate when we leave the pup alone and/or at night. 

Medical status:
Healthy as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP and Bordetella vaccines, spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. (For dogs under 4 months old, adopters will need to finish the DHPP vaccine series and administer the Rabies vaccine at 16 weeks of age.)

How did this dog end up with Social Tees?
Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

PLEASE NOTE: We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses. 

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

LEARN MORE ABOUT US: socialteesnyc.org and Instagram @socialteesnyc

She enjoys walking in the rain, going to the park early in the morning or late at night, and cuddling during movie nights. She is a dog that would do best in a quiet home that has no children as she can be fearful of loud sudden noises in the home."

INTERMEDIATE – As an adult, this dog will need significant structure and plenty of daily exercise, training, and mental stimulation – 90 consecutive minutes of movement in the morning plus potty break walks and brain games throughout the day. Please email fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a t socialteesnyc.org Their foster says: "Mallow is an absolute joy—a sweet, affectionate beagle who loves walks, sniffing, meeting new people, receiving belly rubs, cuddling in your arms, and eating his favorite high-value treat: boiled chicken. Prince Mallow is a true extrovert, and everyone who meets him quickly falls in love with him. He enjoys independent time and handles being left alone for a few hours quite well. He is also very interested in mirrors and loves to stare out the window and watch the people outside! When he comes home, he quickly falls asleep and snores like a good pup! Indoors, Mallow finds chew toys comforting, but his absolute favorite inside activity is his snuffle mat; I would recommend incorporating more scent games and enrichment activities for him." Level of dog ownership experience needed: FLEXIBLE – We predict this dog will be low on the challenge scale with regard to exercise and mental stimulation requirements, but seniors tend to need a lot of help and understanding when it comes to lifestyle and veterinary issues. Seniors usually need quiet, calm environments and routines and do not do well with a lot of bustle, change, and rambunctious movement (kids and young playful dogs, for instance). This dog’s adopter will need to be prepared for senior health challenges, which means frequent vet visits and very expensive veterinary bills. (An annual senior blood panel alone costs around $500 in NYC.) Senior care can also take an emotional toll on their humans. Adopting a mature pup is a wonderful thing to do, but it can also be difficult. Energy level: Medium – Mallow loves to walk and needs a home where he has plenty of opportunities to sniff. He is big on "beagling"--catching scents and forgetting everything else. We are currently working on his pulling, so he will need someone patient who takes him on sniff walks. He needs a good balance of mental stimulation and a solid 60 min walk in the morning. Taking Mallow out for a longer morning walk is really helpful so he can get his sniffs in first thing, but since he loves being outside, we try to take him on any other short neighborhood walks too. He's not hyper when he's inside though and settles into napping and snuggling, but if there's an opportuntiy for him to go out and sniff anything, even if it's just for a block, he wants to join! Okay in the city? Adjusting to the city – This is Mallow's first time in the city. When Mallow first arrived in the city, everything was new and overwhelming. He took some time to adjust to loud noises and stairs, but he is a resilient learner. He is currently making great progress on elevator practice, fully walking inside on his own! He's not completely unfazed, but generally does very well. He's been on the subway (during off peak hours) and did great. Potty trained? Yes – No accidents so far! His foster has a backyard that they let him explore, but he seems to prefer going potty on a walk/leash. Comfort level with strangers: Social butterfly – Mallow loves meeting new people. He loves saying hello to everyone he meets, so we are currently working on recall during walks so he isn't so distracted. Social with other dogs? He is definitely more focused on sniffing, but always wants to say hi to other dogs. His foster notes, "He loves to say hi to all dogs on the street of all sizes and ages and gets along with our senior dog." Social with cats? Probably. Seniors are usually mellow enough that they are able to coexist well with cats. Respectful behavior with other animals (cats, small pets, etc.): Not sure – Wants to chase squirrels and birds so may not be a good match for a home with cats, rabbits, etc. Comfortable with children? (ALWAYS requires adult supervision) Yes for most ages – Mallow is incredibly tolerant and has not been mouthy at all since his foster has been with him. He has been very good with kids who want to say hi and pet him on the street. His foster thinks Mallow would make a fantastic family dog, perhaps for age 12 and up. His foster notes he has been a cuddly guy so far, but he hasn't been exposed to younger kids so they don't want to say he's good with them at this point. Mouthy behavior? His forster reports he's not completely past this stage, but it's not a frequent behavior. He loves a bully stick! Separation anxiety? Adjusting – His foster says "He is mostly fine when you leave, he just tries to get out the door when you're going bc I think he has FOMO of not being outside with the sniffs. He has no barking or howling issues so far though." Leash behavior: "He seems to have done leash work before since he prefers to go outside and potty on a leash but he's a puller and zig zagger for the smells. He responds well to pulling correction when you stop and wait until he stops pulling. He seems to understand that not pulling anymore = more walking/sniffs but it is definitely an ongoing work in progress. We're going to work on incorporating some name recall training as well with treats. Because he can pull when following a track, he needs a patient walker who is willing to continue his lead-training." Cuddle bug level: Medium to high: He loves to snuggle in bed and on the couch, but isn't demanding to be in your lap when you're working and is content laying down close by. Jumping on people to say hello? Listens to correction – his foster has only seem him jump when they're getting the leash and he's excited to go outside. Mallow - 8 years, 34lbs, Beagle, Neutered 

This senior angel is eligible to join our foster-to-adopt program. Please email [fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org](mailto:fostertoadopt@socialteesnyc.org) with the animal’s name in the subject line if you are interested! Want to straight up adopt? Submit an adoption application a[t socialteesnyc.org](http://socialteesnyc.org/)

**Their foster says:** "Mallow is an absolute joy—a sweet, affectionate beagle who loves walks, sniffing, meeting new people, receiving belly rubs, cuddling in your arms, and eating his favorite high-value treat: boiled chicken. Prince Mallow is a true extrovert, and everyone who meets him quickly falls in love with him. He enjoys independent time and handles being left alone for a few hours quite well. He is also very interested in mirrors and loves to stare out the window and watch the people outside! When he comes home, he quickly falls asleep and snores like a good pup! Indoors, Mallow finds chew toys comforting, but his absolute favorite inside activity is his snuffle mat; I would recommend incorporating more scent games and enrichment activities for him."

**Level of dog ownership experience needed:** FLEXIBLE – We predict this dog will be low on the challenge scale with regard to exercise and mental stimulation requirements, but seniors tend to need a lot of help and understanding when it comes to lifestyle and veterinary issues. Seniors usually need quiet, calm environments and routines and do not do well with a lot of bustle, change, and rambunctious movement (kids and young playful dogs, for instance). This dog’s adopter will need to be prepared for senior health challenges, which means frequent vet visits and very expensive veterinary bills. (An annual senior blood panel alone costs around $500 in NYC.) Senior care can also take an emotional toll on their humans. Adopting a mature pup is a wonderful thing to do, but it can also be difficult. 

**Energy level:** Medium **–** Mallow loves to walk and needs a home where he has plenty of opportunities to sniff. He is big on "beagling"--catching scents and forgetting everything else. We are currently working on his pulling, so he will need someone patient who takes him on sniff walks. He needs a good balance of mental stimulation and a solid 60 min walk in the morning. Taking Mallow out for a longer morning walk is really helpful so he can get his sniffs in first thing, but since he loves being outside, we try to take him on any other short neighborhood walks too. He's not hyper when he's inside though and settles into napping and snuggling, but if there's an opportuntiy for him to go out and sniff anything, even if it's just for a block, he wants to join!

**Okay in the city?** Adjusting to the city – This is Mallow's first time in the city. When Mallow first arrived in the city, everything was new and overwhelming. He took some time to adjust to loud noises and stairs, but he is a resilient learner. He is currently making great progress on elevator practice, fully walking inside on his own! He's not completely unfazed, but generally does very well. He's been on the subway (during off peak hours) and did great.

**Potty trained?** Yes – No accidents so far! His foster has a backyard that they let him explore, but he seems to prefer going potty on a walk/leash.

**Comfort level with strangers:** Social butterfly – Mallow loves meeting new people. He loves saying hello to everyone he meets, so we are currently working on recall during walks so he isn't so distracted.

**Social with other dogs?** He is definitely more focused on sniffing, but always wants to say hi to other dogs. His foster notes, "He loves to say hi to all dogs on the street of all sizes and ages and gets along with our senior dog."

**Social with cats?** Probably. Seniors are usually mellow enough that they are able to coexist well with cats. 

**Respectful behavior with other animals (cats, small pets, etc.):** Not sure – Wants to chase squirrels and birds so may not be a good match for a home with cats, rabbits, etc.

**Comfortable with children?** (ALWAYS requires adult supervision) Yes for most ages – Mallow is incredibly tolerant and has not been mouthy at all since his foster has been with him. He has been very good with kids who want to say hi and pet him on the street. His foster thinks Mallow would make a fantastic family dog, perhaps for age 12 and up. His foster notes he has been a cuddly guy so far, but he hasn't been exposed to younger kids so they don't want to say he's good with them at this point.

**Mouthy behavior?** His forster reports he's not completely past this stage, but it's not a frequent behavior. He loves a bully stick!

**Separation anxiety?** Adjusting – His foster says "He is mostly fine when you leave, he just tries to get out the door when you're going bc I think he has FOMO of not being outside with the sniffs. He has no barking or howling issues so far though."

**Leash behavior:** "He seems to have done leash work before since he prefers to go outside and potty on a leash but he's a puller and zig zagger for the smells. He responds well to pulling correction when you stop and wait until he stops pulling. He seems to understand that not pulling anymore = more walking/sniffs but it is definitely an ongoing work in progress. We're going to work on incorporating some name recall training as well with treats. Because he can pull when following a track, he needs a patient walker who is willing to continue his lead-training."

**Cuddle bug level:** Medium to high: He loves to snuggle in bed and on the couch, but isn't demanding to be in your lap when you're working and is content laying down close by.

**Jumping on people to say hello?** Listens to correction – his foster has only seem him jump when they're getting the leash and he's excited to go outside.

**Medical status:** Healthy for their age as far as we know. Up to date on their DHPP, Bordetella, and Rabies vaccines; heartworm tested if coming from Tennessee or Puerto Rico; spayed/neutered; microchipped; treated with dewormer upon intake. Adopters will need to be ready for senior care – at a minimum, that will be annual checkups including senior bloodwork and a dental post adoption (most senior rescues need one).

**How did this dog end up with Social Tees?** Most of our dogs come via partner groups who help us save them from shelters where they are at risk of euthanasia in Tennessee, Los Angeles, and Puerto Rico. There are very few spay/neuter resources there and many more animals in those areas than there are people to adopt them. Rescue groups like ours bring them to the northeast where the desire for pets like these allows us to save their lives. 

**PLEASE NOTE:** We cannot guarantee any breed mix, exact age, or full grown size (if the dog is under a year old). We do our best with very educated guesses.

This animal is not at the Social Tees office, all are in foster homes.

LEARN MORE ABOUT US:[socialteesnyc.org](http://socialteesnyc.org/) and Instagram @socialteesnyc
